title: When AI Takes Notes: Court Allows Privacy Claims Against Otter.ai to Proceed

reading.body:
Otter.ai's transcription service is alleged to have recorded virtual meetings on Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams by default without obtaining consent from all participants, then used these recordings to train its AI systems. The system operated at scale, with the service having recorded over one billion meetings across approximately 25 million users. A federal class-action lawsuit claims this practice violates state and federal privacy and wiretap laws.

The deployment appears to have lacked a check for informed consent from all meeting participants before recording began. Otter's privacy policy required users to check a box to grant permission, but the lawsuit alleges many users remained unaware their conversations would be shared for AI training purposes. The company states it de-identifies data before using it for machine learning, but the suit challenges whether this process is transparent or effective.

It is not established whether Otter's practices violated applicable law, whether the company intentionally obscured its recording practices, or what proportion of users were unaware of the data sharing. The allegations are subject to ongoing litigation.

summary:
# Summary

Otter.ai, a Mountain View-based artificial intelligence company, faces a federal class-action lawsuit alleging it secretly records private work conversations without consent. The suit, filed by Justin Brewer of San Jacinto, California, claims Otter's transcription service records virtual meetings on Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams by default without asking all participants for permission, then uses these recordings to train its AI systems for financial gain. The lawsuit contends this violates state and federal privacy and wiretap laws. Approximately 25 million people currently use Otter's tools, which have recorded over 1 billion meetings since the company's founding in 2016.

The lawsuit highlights concerns about Otter's practices despite the company's privacy policy stating users grant permission by checking a box. The suit alleges many users remain unaware their conversations are shared with Otter for training purposes. Recent complaints on social media describe instances where Otter automatically joined meetings and recorded confidential business discussions. Additionally, the lawsuit questions whether Otter's "de-identification" process effectively anonymizes data before using it for AI improvement. Otter claims it removes identifying information before processing audio for machine learning, but the suit argues the company provides no public explanation of this process.
